terms.grammar: phrase: fīdūcia with the genitive of the reflexive
evidence: Liv. 25.37.12 (Lewis & Short): unde tanta audācia, tanta fīdūcia suī victīs ac fugātīs
terms.comment: Trust in one’s own strength, without the arrogance of cōnfīdentia. Plain fīdūcia is enough where the context shows whose.

terms.grammar: phrase: cōnfīdō with the reflexive dative
terms.comment: The verb, as speech prefers: cōnfīde tibi, have confidence in yourself (see confidence).

evidence: Cic. Rep. 3.42 (Lewis & Short): cōnfīdentiam et vōcem
terms.comment: A false friend more often than not: in a good sense, self-assurance (rare), but much more often boldness, impudence, in comedy and in Cicero’s speeches (Lewis & Short). Quintilian sets it against fīdūcia (11.3.160). Traupman gives it for “smugness” too.

phrases.latin: duās sibi rēs, quōminus in vulgus et in forō dīceret, cōnfīdentiam et vōcem, dēfuisse
phrases.english: that he had lacked two things for speaking to the crowd and in the forum: self-assurance and a voice

phrases.latin: mīrābundī, unde tanta audācia, tanta fīdūcia suī victīs ac fugātīs
phrases.english: wondering where men beaten and put to flight found such daring, such confidence in themselves

sources: Lewis & Short: fiducia · Lewis & Short: confido · Lewis & Short: confidentia
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 150, 157, 158, checked against the searchable text of the book (11 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
